sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for Najdi Arabic (catalog: weight; deciding source Alhammad 2019). Almalki 2020 (Glottolog 592432, listed without description type or URL) turned out to be a George Mason University PhD dissertation with an open copy on CORE (doi:10.13021/mars/5297); downloaded (2.2 MB, 155 pp., text, no scanned) and read. It is a phonetic production/perception study of focus-driven phrasal prominence in Urban Najdi Arabic, not a word-stress study: no stress rule, no weight/foot discussion; its only word-level datum (disyllabic CVV.CVC target words stressed on the initial long-vowel syllable, pp. 32-33) is compatible with but uninformative about the weight coding, so it is silent on the catalog and needs no acquisition priority. this search of works with stress in the title also re-read the 9/16 on-disk Alsuhaibani 2022 (SELT 10(3), doi:10.22158/selt.v10n3p122), whose abstract (p. 122) gives a cleaner unified rule (final-C extrasyllabic; rightmost heavy within the last three syllables, else antepenult / initial in disyllables) and explicitly corrects Alhammad 2019's sub-rule 3; recommended as the deciding quotation, coding unchanged (weight). Alabeeky 2022 (Qassimi Arabic, a Najdi sub-dialect, also held by the project from 9/16) states the same rightmost-heavy-in-window pattern with OT exceptions. GMU MARS/digitalcollections, OATD, DuckDuckGo HTML and the Glossa 5727 page (which cites Almalki) were bot-blocked or empty and were not needed.

new_statements.quote: First, unlike previous studies that employ a three-way weight distinction between light, heavy, and superheavy syllables, a binary weight distinction between light (monomoraic) C(C)v; and heavy (bimoraic) C(C)vX(C) is proposed, where "X" is either a vowel or a consonant. Second, word-final consonants are crucially assumed to be "extrasyllabic". The stress algorithm is constrained so that stress may fall on one of the last three syllables of a word, as follows: Stress the rightmost heavy syllable if and only if it is one of the word's last three syllables; otherwise stress the antepenultimate syllable (initial syllable in disyllabic words).

new_statements.locator: Abstract, p. 122; developed in Section 3 'Syllables and Stress Assignment in NA: Revisited', pp. 126ff; critique of Alhammad (2019) sub-rule 3 in Section 2.2, pp. 125-126
new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive stress with a three-syllable right-edge window: final consonant extrasyllabic; binary light (CV) vs heavy (CVV, CVC, CVVC, CVCC) distinction; stress the rightmost heavy syllable among the last three, else the antepenult (initial in disyllables). This keeps the catalog classification weight unchanged. It differs from the current deciding quote (Alhammad 2019: 'if no heavy syllables are found, stress goes on the first light') in the all-light case for words of four or more syllables (antepenult, not initial) and it explicitly shows Alhammad's sub-rule 3 mispredicting stress in LH.. forms (pp. 125-126). Same venue tier as the catalog source (Scholink vs. CCSE), sole author, Riyadh-based.

audit.recode_to: No change to classification weight / edge=right / what counts as heavy. Refine the primary-stress rule: drop or caveat item (3) 'a lone heavy is stressed wherever it is (ga(ˈlam))' — by Alhammad's own weight criteria final CVC is light, and Alqahtani 2014 (['ki.tab] 'he wrote', p.133), Alsuhaibani 2022 (p.125, 'stress in these examples actually falls on the initial syllable') and Alshammari 2023 NNA ([ˈki.tab], [ˈga.ʕad]) give initial stress for LL(C) disyllables; and restate the default as 'antepenult (initial in di- and trisyllables); stress never precedes the antepenult' (Alqahtani 2014 (4.34-V) p.133; Alsuhaibani 2022 (5b) p.129, data (29) HLLL /(ʔal).(ʔú).(ma).(ra)/), rather than 'leftmost light syllable', which is only exemplified by 2-3-syllable words in Alhammad. Optionally add Alabeeky 2022's [ʔal.ʕa.ˈsˤir]/[ʔa.ˈʕa.rif] classes to exceptions.

sources.quote: pp.99-100: 'QA, as a subdialect of NA, is considered to have an undistinguishable stress pattern from those of other NA dialects. Some works on NA stress (e.g., Prochazka, 1988; Ingham, 1994; Al Amro, 2019) stated that syllable weight and position are the clues to stress placement and agreed on the following set of ordered rules: 1) Stress falls on one of the last three syllables. sources.quote: [p. 4] the term prosodic prominence is defined as a property that makes a word or grouping of words stand out (through acoustic means) relative to other words in the sentence, constituting what is commonly referred to as phrasal stress (or stress beyond the word level) [pp. 32-33] All target words are disyllabic, with the lexical stress falling on the first syllable. ... As shown in Table 4, each target word has two syllables, and the first syllable carries the lexical stress. The vowel on the first syllable of each target word is consistently a long vowel. [Table 4 examples: θa:mir, ha:waʃ, sa:rah, sa:lim, sa:maħ, ri:ma]
sources.locator: Ch. 1 p. 3-4 (definition of 'prosodic prominence' as phrasal stress); Ch. 3 pp. 32-33 (target-word design, Table 4)
sources.note: The dissertation is an acoustic/perception study of sentence-level (focus) prominence in Urban Najdi Arabic: duration, max intensity, F0 max and F0 range measured on the stressed vowel of target words under different focus conditions, plus two prominence-rating perception experiments. It states no word-stress rule and does not discuss syllable weight, feet or the Najdi stress literature (Ingham is cited only for information structure, 2010). tone.quote: The pitch changes at the nucleus which are classed as falling or rising are called tones. … The pitches of the auditory voice which revolve around these three lines exhibit the tones of the language under investigation. … In order to determine the tones of any language it is necessary to describe their pitch movements. Generally speaking, and in line with Halliday (1970), one has to isolate four main tones: Tone 1 falling: medium fall, high fall, shallow fall Tone 2 rising Tone 3 rising falling Tone 4 shallow rise
